title: Paediatric emergencies essentials
summary: What an adult ICU resident needs when a sick child arrives: paediatric resuscitation and weight-based doses, sepsis and fluids, airway sizes and ventilation, bronchiolitis and croup, DKA, and safe transfer to a PICU — with worked doses for 10–20 kg children and Indian context.

topics.title: PALS and weight-based doses
topics.summary: Paediatric cardiac arrest (AHA/AAP 2025), bradycardia and SVT, weight estimation and the core resuscitation doses — with worked examples for a 10 kg and 20 kg child.

definition.text: PALS applies from infancy to 18 years (excluding newborns at birth). Most paediatric arrests are secondary to respiratory failure or shock, so oxygenation, ventilation and early adrenaline for non-shockable rhythms matter most.

steps.title: Recognise and start CPR
steps.detail: Unresponsive, not breathing normally, no definite pulse within 10 s (or HR <60/min with poor perfusion despite oxygenation and ventilation) → start CPR. Push hard and fast: 100–120/min, depth at least one-third of the AP chest diameter (~4 cm infant, ~5 cm child), full recoil, minimal interruptions. Two rescuers: 15:2.

steps.title: Attach monitor/defibrillator; check rhythm
steps.detail: Shockable (VF/pVT) → shock 2 J/kg (2–4 J/kg acceptable), resume CPR immediately for 2 min. Non-shockable (asystole/PEA) → adrenaline as soon as possible.

steps.title: IV or IO access
steps.detail: Rapid IV or IO — choose whichever is fastest; IO in the proximal tibia if IV is not quick. Endotracheal drug route is a last resort.

steps.title: Adrenaline
steps.detail: 0.01 mg/kg IV/IO (0.1 mL/kg of 0.1 mg/mL), max 1 mg. Non-shockable: give as early as possible. Shockable: after 2 shocks, or earlier only if defibrillation is not possible.

steps.title: Escalate shocks and antiarrhythmic
steps.detail: Second shock 4 J/kg; subsequent ≥4 J/kg up to 10 J/kg or adult maximum. Refractory VF/pVT: amiodarone 5 mg/kg (max 300 mg) or lidocaine 1 mg/kg.

steps.title: Airway and ventilation
steps.detail: Bag-mask ventilation is acceptable; with an advanced airway give 1 breath every 2–3 s (20–30/min) with continuous compressions; avoid hyperventilation. Use waveform capnography.

steps.title: Treat reversible causes
steps.detail: Hypoxia (commonest), hypovolaemia, hydrogen ion (acidosis), hypo/hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, hypothermia; tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis. Check glucose in every arrest.

steps.title: Post-arrest care
steps.detail: Avoid fever (>37.5 °C) in comatose children; keep systolic and mean BP above the 10th percentile for age; normoxia (SpO₂ 94–99%) and normocapnia; EEG monitoring if available; multimodal prognostication, not a single test.

redFlags.text: Bradycardia <60/min with poor perfusion in a child = start CPR; it is usually hypoxic — oxygenate and ventilate first.
10-fold dosing errors are the commonest paediatric drug catastrophe: read the weight aloud, confirm mg/kg and mg/mL with a second person.
Do not give routine calcium or sodium bicarbonate in arrest — only for specific indications (hyperkalaemia, hypocalcaemia, CCB or TCA toxicity).
ETCO₂ alone must not be used to decide when to stop resuscitation in children.

pitfalls.text: Delaying adrenaline in non-shockable arrest while securing the airway: give it as soon as access is obtained.
Stacked shocks: paediatric guidance favours a single shock followed immediately by 2 min of CPR.
Giving adenosine through a distal hand cannula without a rapid flush: it is metabolised before reaching the heart.

pearls.text: If an arterial line is in place during CPR, target diastolic BP ≥25 mmHg in infants and ≥30 mmHg in children ≥1 year (AHA/AAP 2025).
New in 2025: IV sotalol may be considered for SVT with cardiopulmonary compromise refractory to vagal manoeuvres, adenosine and cardioversion when expert help is unavailable.

algorithm.title: Paediatric cardiac arrest (AHA/AAP 2025)
algorithm.description: Simplified pulseless arrest algorithm for infants and children.

nodes.text: Unresponsive, no normal breathing, no pulse (or HR <60 with poor perfusion)
Start CPR 15:2, give oxygen, attach monitor/defibrillator
Rhythm shockable?
Shock 2 J/kg → CPR 2 min; obtain IV/IO
Still shockable at rhythm check?
Shock 4 J/kg → CPR 2 min; adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg every 3–5 min
Still shockable?
Shock ≥4 J/kg (max 10 J/kg or adult dose) → CPR 2 min; amiodarone 5 mg/kg or lidocaine 1 mg/kg; treat reversible causes
Non-shockable: adrenaline 0.01 mg/kg IV/IO as soon as possible, then every 3–5 min; CPR 2 min cycles; consider advanced airway
Treat Hs and Ts: hypoxia, hypovolaemia, acidosis, K⁺, glucose, temperature, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins, thrombosis
Signs of ROSC?
Post-cardiac arrest care: avoid fever, BP >10th centile, SpO₂ 94–99%, normocapnia
Continue CPR cycles; reassess rhythm every 2 min; consider ECPR in selected cases where available

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Paediatric arrest is usually the end of progressive hypoxia or shock (asphyxial arrest), which is why the commonest initial rhythms are bradycardia, PEA and asystole. Children have a higher metabolic rate, smaller functional residual capacity and desaturate quickly; good-quality ventilation and early adrenaline (coronary perfusion via alpha-1 vasoconstriction) are central.
consultantNotes.evidence:
**AHA/AAP 2025 PALS — key changes and reaffirmations**
- Early adrenaline for initial non-shockable rhythms is associated with better outcomes (COR 2a).
- For shockable rhythms, defibrillation is the priority; adrenaline after 2 shocks or sooner only if defibrillation is not possible.
- With an arterial line, diastolic BP ≥25 mmHg (infants) and ≥30 mmHg (≥1 year) are included as CPR-quality targets.
- With an advanced airway, ventilate 20–30 breaths/min (1 breath every 2–3 s).
- Initial defibrillation 2–4 J/kg (2 J/kg for ease of teaching), then 4 J/kg, up to 10 J/kg or adult maximum.
- Routine sodium bicarbonate and calcium are not recommended.
- After ROSC: prevent fever (>37.5 °C) in comatose children; keep SBP/MAP above the 10th centile for age.
- Weight-based dosing should not exceed adult doses; length-based tapes are acceptable when weight is unknown.
- IV sotalol is a new option for refractory SVT with compromise when expert help is unavailable.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- Optimal adrenaline interval (observational data conflict).
- Amiodarone vs lidocaine for refractory VF — no clear difference in survival.
- Age formulas vs length-based tapes in children with malnutrition or obesity.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Weight-for-age formulas derived in Western children often **overestimate** weight in undernourished Indian children; weigh the child or use a length tape, and use actual weight for dosing.
- Keep a pre-calculated paediatric resuscitation chart (by weight band) on every emergency trolley — mixing errors with 1 mg/mL adrenaline ampoules are common.
- IO needles may not be stocked in smaller hospitals: an 18G spinal or bone-marrow needle is a recognised improvisation in the proximal tibia when nothing else is available.
- Common Indian precipitants: severe dehydration from diarrhoea, pneumonia, dengue shock, scorpion sting myocarditis, OP poisoning, drowning.

topics.title: Paediatric sepsis and fluids
topics.summary: Phoenix sepsis criteria, the first-hour bundle from the Surviving Sepsis Campaign paediatric guideline, how much fluid to give (and when not to), vasoactive choice, maintenance fluids, and Indian special cases.

definition.text: Phoenix criteria (2024, children <18 years): sepsis = suspected infection with a Phoenix Sepsis Score ≥2 (respiratory, cardiovascular, coagulation and neurological dysfunction); septic shock = sepsis with ≥1 cardiovascular point (severe hypotension for age, lactate >5 mmol/L, or any vasoactive medication). SIRS criteria are no longer used.

steps.title: Recognise
steps.detail: Suspected infection plus abnormal perfusion (prolonged capillary refill, cold or mottled peripheries, weak pulses), altered mental state, tachycardia/tachypnoea out of proportion, hypotension, or raised lactate. Phoenix criteria: sepsis = Phoenix Sepsis Score ≥2; septic shock = sepsis with ≥1 cardiovascular point.

steps.title: ABC, oxygen, access, glucose
steps.detail: High-flow oxygen, monitor, IV or IO access (two if possible), bedside glucose (treat <3 mmol/L / 54 mg/dL with 2–5 mL/kg D10), blood gas with lactate, cultures if they do not delay antibiotics.

steps.title: Antibiotics
steps.detail: Septic shock: broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour. Sepsis-associated organ dysfunction without shock: within 3 hours after appropriate evaluation. Typical empirical: ceftriaxone (add per local antibiogram; include doxycycline/azithromycin if scrub typhus suspected).

steps.title: Fluids — titrate, do not 'pour'
steps.detail: Where intensive care is available: 10–20 mL/kg boluses of balanced crystalloid, reassessing after each, up to 40–60 mL/kg in the first hour, stopping at signs of fluid overload (crackles, hepatomegaly, worsening work of breathing, rising JVP). Without intensive care and without hypotension: no bolus — start maintenance. Without intensive care but with hypotension: up to 40 mL/kg in the first hour.

steps.title: Vasoactive
steps.detail: After 40–60 mL/kg or earlier if overloaded: adrenaline or noradrenaline (rather than dopamine); can be started in dilute form through a good peripheral IV/IO while central access is obtained. Cold shock → adrenaline favoured; warm shock → noradrenaline favoured (individualise).

steps.title: Refractory shock
steps.detail: Hydrocortisone if fluid- and catecholamine-refractory (especially if steroid-dependent or adrenal insufficiency suspected); echo to look for myocardial dysfunction, tamponade, pneumothorax; correct ionised calcium and glucose; source control; refer to PICU/ECMO centre.

steps.title: Maintenance fluids
steps.detail: Use isotonic fluid (e.g. Ringer's lactate or 0.9% saline with dextrose) at Holliday–Segar rates (4/2/1 mL/kg/h), often restricted to ~70% in pneumonia, meningitis or SIADH risk; monitor sodium and avoid fluid overload.

redFlags.text: Crackles, gallop or a liver edge that moves down after a bolus = fluid overload: stop fluids and start a vasoactive.
Hypotension is a late sign in children; tachycardia, prolonged capillary refill and altered sensorium come first.
Purpuric rash with fever = meningococcaemia until proven otherwise: antibiotics immediately.
Severe acute malnutrition with shock: give only small, slow volumes (WHO: 15 mL/kg over 1 h) and watch for heart failure.

pitfalls.text: Giving 60 mL/kg 'by protocol' in a hospital without ventilators or PICU: FEAST showed boluses increased mortality in children without hypotension in resource-limited settings.
Using hypotonic (0.18% or 0.45%) saline for maintenance: risk of hyponatraemic encephalopathy; use isotonic fluids.
Waiting for central access before starting a vasoactive: dilute adrenaline/noradrenaline can run peripherally or via IO while access is obtained.

pearls.text: Reassess after every bolus using the same five things: heart rate, capillary refill, mental state, liver edge and lung crackles.
Balanced crystalloids are suggested over 0.9% saline for resuscitation; albumin is not suggested as first-line.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Children with septic shock more often present with **low cardiac output, high SVR ('cold shock')** than adults, especially infants and in community-acquired sepsis; adults more often have vasodilated 'warm shock'. Myocardial dysfunction, capillary leak and absolute/relative hypovolaemia coexist, so fluid responsiveness is lost early and overload develops easily.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- **SSC Paediatric 2020** (77 recommendations): antibiotics within 1 h for shock, 3 h for sepsis without shock; fluid strategy depends on ICU availability; balanced crystalloids; adrenaline or noradrenaline rather than dopamine; hydrocortisone not routinely; measure lactate.
- **FEAST (2011):** in 3,141 African children with severe febrile illness and impaired perfusion (but not hypotension), 20–40 mL/kg boluses of saline or albumin increased 48-h mortality (10.5–10.6% vs 7.3% without bolus). Mechanisms likely include cardiovascular collapse after transient improvement; the result shaped the 'no bolus without ICU and without hypotension' recommendation.
- **Phoenix criteria (2024):** derived and validated in >3 million encounters across high- and low-resource settings; replaced the 2005 IPSCC SIRS-based definitions.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- Volume of initial fluid in middle-income settings with some ICU capacity (most Indian district hospitals sit between the SSC 'with' and 'without' ICU categories).
- Applicability of FEAST (high malaria and anaemia prevalence) to Indian children.
- Early vasoactive vs further fluids in dengue shock (different pathophysiology: plasma leak).
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- **Dengue shock** in children follows WHO/national dengue protocols (graded crystalloid infusion with haematocrit monitoring) rather than generic sepsis boluses — see the tropical and monsoon fevers module.
- **Scrub typhus** is a common cause of paediatric sepsis with multi-organ dysfunction in India — add doxycycline or azithromycin when suspected (eschar, hepatosplenomegaly, monsoon season).
- **Severe acute malnutrition**: WHO advises 15 mL/kg over 1 h (Ringer's lactate with 5% dextrose, or half-normal saline with 5% dextrose), reassessing for overload; blood transfusion if no improvement.
- Many paediatric wards lack infusion pumps — use burettes/microdrip sets (60 drops = 1 mL) and calculate drops/min carefully.

topics.title: Paediatric airway: sizes, RSI and first ventilator settings
topics.summary: Endotracheal tube size and depth, laryngoscope blades and supraglottic airways by age/weight, a safe paediatric rapid sequence intubation, and lung-protective initial ventilation per PALICC-2.

definition.text: The infant airway is anatomically different: large occiput, large tongue, high anterior larynx, floppy omega-shaped epiglottis, and the narrowest functional point at the cricoid/subglottis. Cuffed tubes are now preferred for all ages beyond the newborn, with cuff pressure monitoring.

steps.title: Decide and call for help
steps.detail: Indications: failure to maintain/protect airway, refractory hypoxaemia or hypercapnia on HFNC/NIV, exhaustion, GCS ≤8, shock needing controlled ventilation, safe transfer. Call the most experienced airway operator available; children decompensate fast.

steps.title: Calculate sizes aloud
steps.detail: Cuffed ETT ID = (age/4) + 3.5; uncuffed = (age/4) + 4. Keep one size above and below. Oral depth (cm at lips) = 3 × ID or (age/2) + 12. Write the weight, tube size, depth and drug doses on a whiteboard.

steps.title: Prepare
steps.detail: Suction (Yankauer + catheter 2 × ETT ID in Fr), bag-valve-mask of correct size, appropriate blade, stylet, bougie, SGA one size ready, waveform capnography, oral airway, NG tube. Fluid bolus 10–20 mL/kg drawn up and adrenaline (push-dose or infusion) ready if shocked.

steps.title: Preoxygenate
steps.detail: Head position (shoulder roll in infants, sniffing in older child); 100% O₂ by mask for 3 min, or HFNC/NIV if already on it; continue apnoeic oxygenation via nasal cannula during laryngoscopy.

steps.title: Induce and paralyse
steps.detail: Ketamine 1–2 mg/kg (0.5–1 mg/kg in profound shock) ± fentanyl 1–2 mcg/kg; rocuronium 1–1.2 mg/kg. Atropine 0.02 mg/kg is not routine; consider for bradycardia or in infants receiving suxamethonium.

steps.title: Intubate and confirm
steps.detail: Video laryngoscope if available. Gentle bag-mask ventilation (low pressure) is acceptable if desaturating. Confirm with sustained waveform ETCO₂, chest rise and auscultation; cuff pressure <20–25 cmH₂O; chest X-ray for tip position (mid-trachea, T2–T3).

steps.title: Plan B/C
steps.detail: If two attempts fail: oxygenate with bag-mask + adjuncts or an SGA, call for help. Cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate: in children <8 years needle cricothyroidotomy (cannula) with jet/bag oxygenation as a bridge; surgical airway in older children. Keep the drawn-up dose list for re-attempts.

steps.title: Initial ventilation (PALICC-2)
steps.detail: Tidal volume 5–8 mL/kg predicted (ideal) weight; 3–6 mL/kg if poor compliance. Plateau ≤28 cmH₂O; driving pressure ≤15 cmH₂O; PEEP 5–8 then titrate to oxygenation and haemodynamics. SpO₂ 92–97% (88–92% acceptable in severe PARDS with PEEP ≥10). Permissive hypercapnia with pH ≥7.20, except in raised ICP or pulmonary hypertension.

redFlags.text: Bradycardia during laryngoscopy = hypoxia until proven otherwise: stop, oxygenate with bag-mask, then reattempt.
Post-intubation arrest risk is high in shock: resuscitate first and have fluids and adrenaline ready before induction.
Sudden deterioration in a ventilated child — DOPE: Displacement, Obstruction, Pneumothorax, Equipment failure. Disconnect and hand-bag with 100% O₂.
Drooling, tripod posture, toxic look and soft stridor suggest epiglottitis: do not lie the child flat or examine the throat; get the most senior anaesthetist and ENT.

pitfalls.text: Over-inflating the cuff: subglottic stenosis risk; measure cuff pressure with a manometer, keep <20–25 cmH₂O.
Endobronchial intubation is common because the trachea is short (~4–5 cm in infants); listen in both axillae and check depth after every move.
Hyperventilating with the bag after intubation: drops venous return and causes hypocapnia; ventilate gently at an age-appropriate rate.

pearls.text: Use a written paediatric intubation checklist and say the tube size, depth and drug doses aloud before induction — it reduces 10-fold and size errors.
Gastric distension from bag-mask ventilation splints the diaphragm in infants — place an NG/OG tube early after intubation.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Infants have a high oxygen consumption (6–8 mL/kg/min vs 3–4 mL/kg/min in adults) and small FRC, so safe apnoea time is very short. Poiseuille's law means 1 mm of oedema in an infant's 4 mm subglottis increases resistance about 16-fold — explaining why croup and post-extubation stridor are dangerous.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- **Cuffed vs uncuffed tubes:** Weiss et al. 2009 (2,246 children <5 years, multicentre RCT) found cuffed tubes reduced tube exchanges (2.1% vs 30.8%) without increasing post-extubation stridor (4.4% vs 4.7%). AHA 2020/2025 supports cuffed tubes for infants and children.
- **Cricoid pressure** is not recommended routinely during paediatric intubation (AHA 2020/2025).
- **Atropine premedication** is not recommended routinely; reserve for bradycardia risk.
- **PALICC-2 (2023):** PARDS defined by OI/OSI on invasive ventilation (or P/F, S/F on non-invasive support); recommendations for tidal volume by compliance, plateau ≤28 cmH₂O, driving pressure ≤15 cmH₂O, SpO₂ targets, conservative fluids after resuscitation, and prone positioning considered in severe PARDS.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- Video vs direct laryngoscopy as first-line in children (first-pass success better for novices with VL).
- Ketamine vs etomidate in shock (etomidate rarely stocked in Indian paediatric units; adrenal suppression concerns in sepsis).
- High-frequency oscillatory ventilation in severe PARDS — no recommendation as routine.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Cuffed paediatric tubes, size-appropriate video laryngoscope blades and paediatric ETCO₂ adapters may not be available in district hospitals — this is a reason to refer early to a PICU centre.
- Keep a paediatric airway trolley with a laminated size chart; many emergencies in Indian general ICUs involve teenagers (OP poisoning, snakebite, trauma) who can be managed with adult-sized equipment by weight.
- Suxamethonium remains widely used in India; avoid in hyperkalaemia, neuromuscular disease and burns >48 h, and give atropine in infants.

topics.title: Bronchiolitis and croup
topics.summary: Two common respiratory emergencies of infancy: bronchiolitis (supportive care, oxygen thresholds, HFNC/CPAP, what not to give) and croup (steroids for all, nebulised adrenaline for stridor at rest, and the dangerous mimics including diphtheria).

definition.text: Bronchiolitis is a viral (mostly RSV) lower respiratory tract infection of infants causing small-airway inflammation and obstruction. Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis, mostly parainfluenza) causes subglottic oedema.

steps.title: Which one is it?
steps.detail: **Bronchiolitis**: <2 years (peak 3–6 months), coryza then cough, tachypnoea, recession, fine crackles ± wheeze, poor feeding. **Croup**: usually 6 months–3 years, barking cough, hoarse voice, inspiratory stridor, worse at night, often low fever. Toxic look, drooling or no barking cough → think epiglottitis, bacterial tracheitis, diphtheria, foreign body.

steps.title: Oxygen and feeding
steps.detail: Give oxygen if SpO₂ persistently <90% (≥6 weeks old, no underlying condition) or <92% (<6 weeks or with underlying conditions). Suction nose only if secretions cause distress or feeding difficulty. If oral intake <50–75% of usual: NG/OG feeds; IV isotonic fluids only if NG not tolerated or impending respiratory failure.

steps.title: Escalate respiratory support
steps.detail: Rising work of breathing or hypoxaemia despite low-flow O₂: HFNC (commonly 2 L/kg/min) as rescue; CPAP for impending respiratory failure; intubate for apnoea, exhaustion or failure of CPAP. Monitor with continuous SpO₂ and a blood gas (capillary acceptable).

steps.title: What NOT to give
steps.detail: No routine salbutamol, adrenaline, ipratropium, hypertonic saline, montelukast, corticosteroids or antibiotics (unless secondary bacterial infection suspected). No routine chest X-ray or blood tests.

steps.title: Steroid for every croup
steps.detail: Dexamethasone 0.15–0.6 mg/kg orally once (IM/IV if vomiting); 0.15 mg/kg is effective for mild–moderate croup. Alternative: nebulised budesonide 2 mg (e.g. if vomiting), or oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg. Keep the child calm on the parent's lap; avoid distressing interventions.

steps.title: Stridor at rest
steps.detail: Moderate–severe croup (stridor at rest, recession): nebulised adrenaline 0.5 mL/kg of 1 mg/mL (1:1000), max 5 mL, with oxygen; may repeat. Observe at least 2–4 h after adrenaline for rebound.

steps.title: Impending respiratory failure
steps.detail: Agitation or lethargy, cyanosis, decreasing air entry, reduced stridor with tiring: call senior anaesthetist/ENT, give oxygen and adrenaline nebs, intubate in theatre/controlled setting with a tube 0.5–1 mm smaller than predicted.

redFlags.text: Apnoea in a young infant with bronchiolitis — especially <6–8 weeks or ex-preterm — needs HDU/PICU-level monitoring.
Bronchiolitis: SpO₂ <92% on oxygen, grunting, marked recession, RR >70, exhaustion or rising PCO₂ = escalate (HFNC/CPAP) and refer.
Croup with quiet stridor, falling SpO₂ and drowsiness is pre-arrest — not improvement.
Grey adherent membrane, bull neck, unimmunised child = diphtheria: isolate, give antitoxin and antibiotics, monitor ECG for myocarditis.

pitfalls.text: Treating bronchiolitis with salbutamol 'trial after trial': no benefit and causes tachycardia; NICE and AAP advise against bronchodilators.
Discharging croup straight after nebulised adrenaline: the effect lasts ~2 h; observe for at least 2–4 h.
Distressing a croupy child (separating from parent, painful procedures, examining the throat) can precipitate complete obstruction.

pearls.text: Bronchiolitis typically worsens to a peak on days 3–5 of illness — warn parents and plan admission thresholds accordingly.

PARIS (2018): HFNC used as initial support in ward infants with bronchiolitis reduced escalation of care compared with standard oxygen, without reducing ICU admission, length of stay or oxygen duration.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Bronchiolitis: epithelial necrosis, mucus plugging and oedema of small airways → air trapping, atelectasis, V/Q mismatch and increased work of breathing; infants tire and develop apnoea (especially young/premature). Croup: subglottic oedema at the narrowest part of the child's airway; resistance rises with the fourth power of the radius reduction, and agitation increases turbulent flow.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- **NICE NG9 (2015, updated 2021)** and **AAP 2014**: supportive care only; oxygen thresholds 90%/92%; no bronchodilators, steroids, hypertonic saline (in the ED), antibiotics or routine investigations; consider CPAP for impending respiratory failure.
- **PARIS (Franklin, NEJM 2018):** 1,472 infants <12 months on wards in Australia/NZ; treatment failure requiring escalation 12% with HFNC vs 23% with standard oxygen; ICU admission (about 12% vs 14%), length of stay and duration of oxygen did not differ significantly.
- **Croup steroids (Cochrane 2018, 43 trials):** glucocorticoids reduce symptoms at 2 h, return visits and length of stay. **Bjornson 2004 (NEJM):** single oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg reduced return visits in mild croup (7.3% vs 15.3%). Lower dose 0.15 mg/kg appears comparable in several trials.
- **Nebulised adrenaline** relieves symptoms within 30 min; effect wanes by 2 h, without true 'rebound' worsening below baseline.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- HFNC as first-line vs rescue in bronchiolitis (cost, crowding, 'treatment creep').
- Optimal croup dexamethasone dose (0.15 vs 0.6 mg/kg).
- Nirsevimab and maternal RSV vaccination for prevention — not widely available in India yet.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- **Diphtheria** still occurs in India, particularly in under-immunised communities and outbreaks; always ask about immunisation and look at the throat in a calm setting if diphtheria is suspected (but not if epiglottitis is). Diphtheria antitoxin (DAT) is dosed by severity (roughly 20,000–100,000 units — verify with current national/CDC guidance) and is often scarce; inform public health.
- Bubble CPAP is a low-cost, effective option for bronchiolitis and pneumonia in Indian district hospitals.
- Dexamethasone injection (4 mg/mL) is cheap and universally available and can be given orally.

topics.title: Paediatric diabetic ketoacidosis
topics.summary: ISPAD 2022-based management of DKA in children and adolescents: severity, cautious fluid deficit replacement over 24–48 h, insulin 0.05–0.1 unit/kg/h without bolus, potassium rules, the two-bag dextrose approach and recognising and treating cerebral oedema.

definition.text: DKA results from absolute or relative insulin deficiency with counter-regulatory hormone excess, producing hyperglycaemia, osmotic diuresis, ketoacidosis and total-body depletion of water, sodium, potassium and phosphate. It is the leading cause of death in children with type 1 diabetes, mostly from cerebral oedema.

steps.title: Confirm and grade
steps.detail: DKA = glucose >11 mmol/L (>200 mg/dL) + venous pH <7.3 or HCO₃⁻ <18 mmol/L + ketonaemia (β-hydroxybutyrate ≥3 mmol/L) or moderate/large ketonuria. Mild: pH <7.3 or HCO₃⁻ <18; moderate: pH <7.2 or HCO₃⁻ <10; severe: pH <7.1 or HCO₃⁻ <5. Weigh the child.

steps.title: Resuscitate only if shocked
steps.detail: Shock (weak pulses, hypotension, CRT >3 s): 0.9% saline 20 mL/kg rapidly, repeat as needed. No shock but dehydrated: 10–20 mL/kg 0.9% saline over 20–30 min.

steps.title: Deficit + maintenance
steps.detail: Estimate deficit (moderate DKA ~5–7%, severe ~7–10% of body weight) and replace evenly over 24–48 h plus maintenance, using 0.45–0.9% saline or a balanced crystalloid with potassium. Avoid exceeding ~1.5–2 × maintenance in most children.

steps.title: Insulin infusion — no bolus
steps.detail: Start regular insulin 0.05–0.1 unit/kg/h at least 1 h after starting fluids (0.05 unit/kg/h in young children or mild DKA is reasonable). Do not reduce below 0.05 unit/kg/h until acidosis resolves; add dextrose instead.

steps.title: Potassium
steps.detail: Hypokalaemic: add potassium from the start (with initial volume expansion), before insulin. Normal K⁺: add potassium when insulin starts. Hyperkalaemic: wait until urine output is documented. Usually 40 mmol/L (20 mmol/L if rate >10 mL/kg/h); keep ≤0.5 mmol/kg/h.

steps.title: Add dextrose
steps.detail: When glucose falls to ~14–17 mmol/L (250–300 mg/dL) or drops faster than 5 mmol/L/h: add 5% dextrose (up to 10–12.5%) to keep glucose 8–12 mmol/L (145–220 mg/dL) while insulin clears ketones.

steps.title: Monitor
steps.detail: Hourly glucose, vitals, neurological observations (headache, behaviour, GCS) and fluid balance; venous gas, electrolytes and ketones every 2–4 h. Corrected sodium should rise as glucose falls — a falling corrected Na⁺ is a warning sign.

steps.title: Switch to subcutaneous insulin
steps.detail: Resolved when pH >7.30, HCO₃⁻ >18 mmol/L and β-hydroxybutyrate <1 mmol/L, tolerating oral intake. Give SC rapid-acting insulin 15–30 min (regular 1–2 h) before stopping the infusion; start basal insulin.

redFlags.text: Headache, vomiting, irritability, bradycardia with rising BP, falling GCS, incontinence or sudden drop in SpO₂ = cerebral oedema until proven otherwise: treat immediately, do not wait for CT.
Severe DKA, age <5 years, new-onset diabetes, high urea, low PCO₂ and bicarbonate use are risk factors for cerebral oedema.
K⁺ <3 mmol/L: delay insulin and give potassium first (cardiac monitor).
Arrhythmias from hypo/hyperkalaemia: put every moderate/severe DKA child on ECG monitoring.

pitfalls.text: Giving an insulin bolus or starting insulin with the first bolus: increases the risk of rapid osmolar shifts and hypokalaemia; wait at least 1 h, no bolus.
Turning insulin off when glucose normalises: ketoacidosis persists — add dextrose and keep insulin at ≥0.05 unit/kg/h.
Routine sodium bicarbonate: associated with cerebral oedema; reserve for pH <6.9 with poor cardiac contractility or life-threatening hyperkalaemia.

pearls.text: Two-bag system (one bag with dextrose, one without, same electrolytes) lets nurses change dextrose concentration by adjusting two rates without new bags.

PECARN FLUID (2018): in 1,389 episodes, neither faster vs slower rehydration nor 0.9% vs 0.45% saline changed rates of clinically apparent brain injury (~0.9%) — the focus is careful monitoring rather than fluid restriction.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Insulin deficiency and glucagon excess drive hepatic gluconeogenesis and lipolysis → ketone production (β-hydroxybutyrate > acetoacetate) and high anion gap acidosis. Osmotic diuresis depletes water, sodium, potassium and phosphate; serum K⁺ may be normal or high despite total-body depletion because of acidosis and insulin lack. Cerebral oedema is now thought to relate more to cerebral hypoperfusion and neuroinflammation during the illness than simply to fluid rate.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- **ISPAD 2022 consensus**: biochemical definition and severity grading; fluid deficit replacement over 24–48 h; insulin 0.05–0.1 unit/kg/h from ≥1 h after fluids; potassium timing by initial K⁺; avoid bicarbonate except in specific situations; mannitol or hypertonic saline for cerebral oedema.
- **PECARN FLUID (Kuppermann, NEJM 2018):** 2×2 factorial RCT (faster vs slower; 0.9% vs 0.45% saline); no significant difference in GCS decline (<14) or clinically apparent brain injury; short-term memory similar. Supports moderately liberal, isotonic-to-half-normal fluids with monitoring.
- **Cerebral oedema** occurs in roughly 0.5–1% of paediatric DKA episodes with substantial mortality; subclinical oedema is common on imaging.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- Insulin 0.05 vs 0.1 unit/kg/h (similar efficacy in small trials; 0.05 suits young children).
- 0.9% saline vs balanced crystalloids (hyperchloraemic acidosis can delay apparent resolution of HCO₃⁻).
- Subtracting resuscitation boluses from total fluid.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- DKA is frequently the **first presentation** of type 1 diabetes in Indian children, often after misdiagnosis as gastroenteritis, pneumonia or acute abdomen; check glucose in every sick, vomiting, breathless child.
- Blood ketone meters are not universal; urine ketones and anion gap are acceptable surrogates, but urine ketones lag behind clearance.
- Many wards lack infusion pumps — paediatric DKA should be managed in an HDU/PICU with syringe drivers; if transfer is needed, start fluids and insulin per protocol before transfer and send the flow chart.
- Insulin is supplied as 40 units/mL (vials) and 100 units/mL (pens/vials) in India — confirm the strength before drawing up to avoid 2.5-fold errors.

topics.title: Safe transfer of a sick child to PICU
topics.summary: Stabilise-then-transfer: deciding when and how to move a critically ill child within or between hospitals, communication with the receiving PICU, team, equipment and oxygen planning, in-transit monitoring and handover — adapted to Indian ambulance realities.

definition.text: Transfer is a period of high risk: intrahospital (to CT, theatre, PICU) and interhospital transfers both carry adverse-event rates that rise with severity of illness and are reduced by checklists, trained teams and standardised equipment.

steps.title: Is transfer needed and is the child safe to move?
steps.detail: Transfer when the child needs care you cannot provide (ventilation, inotropes, dialysis, neurosurgery, ECMO). Risks of the journey must be lower than the risks of staying. Discuss with the receiving PICU consultant early — they can advise on stabilisation before a bed is free.

steps.title: A — airway
steps.detail: If the airway may deteriorate en route (GCS ≤8, worsening work of breathing, refractory shock, status epilepticus, severe croup), intubate before leaving. Confirm tube position on X-ray, record size and depth at lips, secure well, ETCO₂ attached.

steps.title: B and C — breathing and circulation
steps.detail: Transfer ventilator or bag with PEEP valve; NG/OG tube on free drainage. Two secure IV/IO lines; vasoactive infusions running and stable on syringe drivers with spare syringes; resuscitation fluid ready.

steps.title: D, E — glucose, seizures, temperature
steps.detail: Check glucose before leaving and treat <3 mmol/L (54 mg/dL); control seizures; keep infants warm (cap, wraps, warmed ambulance) — hypothermia worsens acidosis and coagulopathy. Splint fractures; cervical immobilisation if trauma.

steps.title: ISBAR call and documents
steps.detail: Doctor-to-doctor call (ISBAR): situation, background, assessment with latest vitals/gas, recommendation and ETA. Send notes, drug chart, fluid chart, imaging (on disk/phone), investigations, consent and referral letter. Explain to parents; one parent usually accompanies.

steps.title: Team, equipment and drugs
steps.detail: Escort: a doctor skilled in paediatric airway and resuscitation plus a trained nurse for any ventilated or unstable child. Portable monitor (ECG, SpO₂, NIBP/arterial line, ETCO₂), suction, age-appropriate airway kit, defibrillator with paediatric pads, pre-calculated drug chart for that weight.

steps.title: Oxygen planning
steps.detail: Oxygen needed (L) = (minute ventilation or flow in L/min + ventilator driving gas) × journey minutes × 2 (safety). Check cylinder sizes and pressures before departure; carry at least 30 min reserve beyond the doubled estimate.

steps.title: Monitor and record
steps.detail: Continuous ECG, SpO₂, ETCO₂ if ventilated, BP at least every 5–15 min; record observations and interventions. Stop the vehicle for procedures if needed. Pre-defined plan for deterioration (DOPE, arrest dose chart).

steps.title: Structured handover
steps.detail: Hands-off, eyes-on handover at the bedside: patient, events, current therapy, outstanding issues; then transfer monitors and infusions one by one.

redFlags.text: Never transfer an unstable child to 'buy time' without stabilisation: transport deaths are usually from airway loss, hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, hypothermia or unrecognised shock.
A child with a deteriorating airway (severe croup, epiglottitis, burns) should be intubated by an expert before transfer — not in a moving ambulance.
Running out of oxygen or syringe-driver battery mid-journey is a preventable death: check and double the estimate.

pitfalls.text: Leaving before the child has been stable on the transport ventilator for 10–15 minutes.
Infusions in gravity drips in the ambulance: rates become unpredictable; use syringe drivers.
No pre-calculated drug chart: dose-calculation errors under stress in a moving vehicle.

pearls.text: 'Scoop and run' is right only for time-critical surgical conditions (e.g. extradural haematoma) once airway and breathing are secured — otherwise 'stay and stabilise'.
A video call or photo of the monitor and X-ray to the receiving PICU consultant often improves pre-transfer stabilisation.

algorithm.title: Transferring a critically ill child
algorithm.description: Stabilise, communicate, equip, monitor, hand over.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Transport adds vibration, acceleration, noise, cramped access, limited oxygen and battery supplies and cold — all of which can destabilise a child with little physiological reserve. Infants lose heat quickly (large surface area-to-weight ratio), and movement can dislodge short endotracheal tubes.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- **ACCM/SCCM guidelines (Warren 2004)** for inter- and intrahospital transport: pre-transport communication, accompanying personnel (minimum two, one a critical care nurse or physician for unstable patients), minimum equipment and monitoring; mostly consensus-based.
- **ISCCM position statement on intrahospital transport (Zirpe 2025)**: risk stratification, checklists, trained teams, equipment standards and documentation for Indian ICUs.
- Adverse events during transport occur in a substantial minority of critically ill transfers; specialist paediatric retrieval teams are associated with fewer critical incidents than non-specialist teams in observational studies.
consultantNotes.controversies:
- Specialist retrieval team vs referring team escort (resource-dependent; specialist teams are rarely available in India outside a few metros).
- Timing: delaying transfer to stabilise vs urgent transfer for definitive care.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Most public '108/102' ambulances in India are basic life support; advanced life support ambulances with ventilators and paediatric equipment are limited and often private — confirm capabilities before departure.
- Long distances and road conditions make journeys longer than expected: plan oxygen, batteries and drugs for at least double the estimated time.
- Families often arrange transport themselves; insist on a trained escort for unstable children and document the risks discussed.
- Keep a printed paediatric transfer checklist and weight-based dose chart in every emergency department and ICU.

quiz.explanation: Allows detection of instability before departure.

drugs.name: Adrenaline (epinephrine) — paediatric
drugs.indications: Cardiac arrest; anaphylaxis; fluid-refractory (cold) septic shock; moderate–severe croup (nebulised); symptomatic bradycardia
drugs.adultDose: Paediatric doses: arrest 0.01 mg/kg IV/IO (= 0.1 mL/kg of 0.1 mg/mL), max 1 mg, every 3–5 min. Anaphylaxis 0.01 mg/kg IM of 1 mg/mL (max 0.5 mg). Infusion 0.05–1 mcg/kg/min. Croup: nebulised 0.5 mL/kg of 1 mg/mL (max 5 mL).
drugs.preparationIndia: 1 mg/mL (1:1000) 1 mL ampoules. Make 0.1 mg/mL by diluting 1 mL in 9 mL NS. Infusion e.g. 0.3 mg/kg in 50 mL: 1 mL/h = 0.1 mcg/kg/min.
drugs.cautions: Confusing 1 mg/mL with 0.1 mg/mL causes 10-fold errors — label syringes. Extravasation risk if given peripherally undiluted.
drugs.verify: Upper infusion limit varies by unit; confirm local PICU protocol.

drugs.name: Amiodarone — paediatric
drugs.indications: Shock-refractory VF/pulseless VT; perfusing wide-complex or refractory SVT (with expert advice)
drugs.adultDose: Arrest: 5 mg/kg IV/IO bolus (max 300 mg), may repeat up to a total of 15 mg/kg. Perfusing tachycardia: 5 mg/kg over 20–60 min.
drugs.preparationIndia: 150 mg/3 mL ampoule; dilute in D5W.
drugs.cautions: Hypotension, bradycardia, QT prolongation; avoid combining with other QT-prolonging drugs without expert input.

drugs.name: Lidocaine (lignocaine) — paediatric
drugs.indications: Shock-refractory VF/pVT (alternative to amiodarone)
drugs.adultDose: 1 mg/kg IV/IO bolus; infusion 20–50 mcg/kg/min.
drugs.preparationIndia: 2% (20 mg/mL) preservative-free for IV use.
drugs.cautions: Seizures and myocardial depression with toxicity.

drugs.name: Adenosine — paediatric
drugs.indications: SVT with a pulse after vagal manoeuvres
drugs.adultDose: 0.1 mg/kg rapid IV push (max 6 mg) with immediate saline flush; second dose 0.2 mg/kg (max 12 mg).
drugs.preparationIndia: 3 mg/mL, 2 mL vials.
drugs.cautions: Give through a large proximal vein with a two-syringe/three-way-tap flush; transient asystole; bronchospasm in asthma.
drugs.monitoring: Continuous ECG recording during the dose.

drugs.name: Atropine — paediatric
drugs.indications: Bradycardia from increased vagal tone or primary AV block; selected intubations at risk of bradycardia
drugs.adultDose: 0.02 mg/kg IV/IO (max single dose 0.5 mg); may repeat once.
drugs.preparationIndia: 0.6 mg/mL ampoules.
drugs.cautions: Not a substitute for oxygenation/ventilation in hypoxic bradycardia (commonest cause in children).

drugs.name: Dextrose 10% — paediatric
drugs.indications: Hypoglycaemia in children (check glucose in every sick child)
drugs.adultDose: 2–5 mL/kg of 10% dextrose IV/IO (0.2–0.5 g/kg); recheck glucose in 15–30 min; then maintenance dextrose.
drugs.preparationIndia: 10% dextrose bags; to make from 25%: 2 parts 25% + 3 parts water/NS (approx. 10%).
drugs.cautions: Avoid 25–50% dextrose peripherally in small children (vein injury); avoid hyperglycaemia.

drugs.name: Calcium chloride / calcium gluconate — paediatric
drugs.indications: Documented hypocalcaemia, hyperkalaemia, calcium-channel blocker toxicity (not routine in arrest)
drugs.adultDose: Calcium chloride 10%: 20 mg/kg (0.2 mL/kg) IV/IO slowly (max 1 g). Calcium gluconate 10%: 60 mg/kg (0.6 mL/kg) IV/IO slowly (max 3 g).
drugs.preparationIndia: Calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL ampoules are the usual Indian presentation; calcium chloride less widely stocked.
drugs.cautions: Severe tissue injury if extravasated (especially chloride); not routine in cardiac arrest (2025 PALS).

drugs.name: Sodium bicarbonate — paediatric
drugs.indications: Hyperkalaemia, sodium-channel blocker (TCA) toxicity; not routine in arrest
drugs.adultDose: 1 mEq/kg slow IV/IO (8.4% = 1 mEq/mL; dilute 1:1 in infants).
drugs.cautions: Not recommended routinely in paediatric arrest; flush line before catecholamines (inactivation).

drugs.name: Balanced crystalloid / 0.9% saline bolus — paediatric
drugs.indications: Septic shock and hypovolaemia
drugs.adultDose: 10–20 mL/kg over 5–20 min, reassess after each bolus; up to 40–60 mL/kg in the first hour where intensive care is available, stopping at signs of fluid overload (crackles, hepatomegaly, rising work of breathing). Balanced crystalloid (Ringer's lactate) suggested over 0.9% saline.
drugs.preparationIndia: Ringer's lactate and 0.9% saline widely available; use 50 mL syringes 'push-pull' for small children.
drugs.cautions: Without intensive care and without hypotension, SSC suggests no bolus (maintenance fluids instead). Severe acute malnutrition: use smaller, slower volumes (WHO).
drugs.monitoring: HR, capillary refill, BP, liver span, crackles, urine output, lactate.

drugs.name: Noradrenaline (norepinephrine) — paediatric
drugs.indications: Warm (vasodilated) septic shock after fluids
drugs.adultDose: 0.05–1 mcg/kg/min IV infusion, titrated to perfusion and age-appropriate MAP.
drugs.preparationIndia: Common paediatric 'rule of 0.3': 0.3 mg/kg in 50 mL; 1 mL/h = 0.1 mcg/kg/min.
drugs.cautions: May start through a good peripheral line in dilute form while central access is obtained (SSC).
drugs.verify: Dose ceiling and peripheral concentration limits per local PICU protocol.

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone — paediatric
drugs.indications: Empirical antibiotic for community-acquired sepsis/meningitis beyond the neonatal period
drugs.adultDose: Sepsis: 50–80 mg/kg IV once daily (max 2 g). Meningitis: 100 mg/kg/day IV in 1–2 doses (max 4 g/day). Give within 1 h of recognising septic shock.
drugs.preparationIndia: 250 mg, 500 mg, 1 g vials.
drugs.cautions: Avoid in neonates with hyperbilirubinaemia and with calcium-containing IV fluids in neonates.
drugs.verify: Confirm local antibiogram (e.g. add vancomycin, cover for scrub typhus/dengue mimics where relevant).

drugs.name: Hydrocortisone — paediatric
drugs.indications: Catecholamine-resistant septic shock with suspected adrenal insufficiency; known adrenal insufficiency/chronic steroid use
drugs.adultDose: Commonly 2 mg/kg IV bolus (max 100 mg), then 1 mg/kg 6-hourly (max 50 mg/dose) or 50–100 mg/m²/day.
drugs.preparationIndia: 100 mg vials.
drugs.cautions: SSC suggests against routine use when fluids and vasopressors restore stability.
drugs.verify: SSC paediatric guideline does not specify a dose; dose shown is common PICU practice — confirm locally.

drugs.name: Ketamine — paediatric
drugs.indications: Induction for intubation in shocked or asthmatic children; procedural sedation
drugs.adultDose: Induction 1–2 mg/kg IV (reduce to 0.5–1 mg/kg in profound shock); IM 4–5 mg/kg if no access.
drugs.preparationIndia: 50 mg/mL vials (10 mL); dilute to 10 mg/mL for children.
drugs.cautions: Laryngospasm and hypersalivation (rare); may still drop BP in catecholamine-depleted shock.

drugs.name: Rocuronium — paediatric
drugs.indications: Rapid sequence intubation
drugs.adultDose: 1–1.2 mg/kg IV.
drugs.preparationIndia: 10 mg/mL (5 mL vials); refrigerate.
drugs.cautions: Only after airway plan and failed-airway backup are ready; sugammadex availability varies.

drugs.name: Fentanyl — paediatric
drugs.indications: Analgesia/blunting response at intubation; post-intubation analgesia
drugs.adultDose: 1–2 mcg/kg IV slowly; infusion 1–4 mcg/kg/h.
drugs.preparationIndia: 50 mcg/mL ampoules.
drugs.cautions: Chest wall rigidity with rapid large doses (infants); hypotension; apnoea.

drugs.name: Dexamethasone (croup)
drugs.indications: Croup (all severities)
drugs.adultDose: 0.15–0.6 mg/kg PO (or IM/IV) single dose; 0.15 mg/kg is effective for mild–moderate croup; 0.6 mg/kg (max about 10–16 mg) often used for severe croup.
drugs.preparationIndia: 0.5 mg tablets; 4 mg/mL injection can be given orally mixed in syrup.
drugs.cautions: Single dose is usually enough.

drugs.name: Budesonide (nebulised)
drugs.indications: Croup when oral route is not tolerated
drugs.adultDose: 2 mg nebulised single dose.
drugs.preparationIndia: 0.5 mg/2 mL respules (use 4 respules = 2 mg).

drugs.name: Regular (soluble) insulin — paediatric DKA
drugs.indications: Paediatric DKA
drugs.adultDose: 0.05–0.1 unit/kg/h IV infusion, started at least 1 h after starting fluid replacement; NO bolus.
drugs.preparationIndia: 100 units/mL vials; 50 units in 50 mL NS = 1 unit/mL (prime the line).
drugs.cautions: Hypokalaemia and hypoglycaemia; start only once K⁺ ≥3.5 mmol/L (ISPAD) or with K⁺ replacement running.
drugs.monitoring: Hourly glucose, 2–4-hourly electrolytes/blood gas, hourly neuro observations.

drugs.name: Potassium chloride (in IV fluids) — paediatric DKA
drugs.indications: Potassium replacement in DKA
drugs.adultDose: Usually 40 mmol/L in rehydration fluid (20 mmol/L if fluid rate >10 mL/kg/h); start with initial volume expansion if hypokalaemic, with insulin if normokalaemic, and after urine output if hyperkalaemic. Keep within 0.5 mmol/kg/h.
drugs.preparationIndia: 15% KCl = 2 mmol/mL (10 mL ampoule = 20 mmol); premixed bags preferred to avoid errors.
drugs.cautions: Never give KCl as an IV bolus; mix bags thoroughly.

drugs.name: Mannitol — paediatric
drugs.indications: Cerebral oedema in DKA (or raised ICP)
drugs.adultDose: 0.5–1 g/kg IV over 10–15 min; may repeat after 30 min if no response.
drugs.preparationIndia: 20% mannitol (200 mg/mL): 0.5–1 g/kg = 2.5–5 mL/kg.
drugs.cautions: Diuresis and hypovolaemia; crystallises if cold.

drugs.name: Hypertonic saline 3% — paediatric
drugs.indications: Cerebral oedema in DKA (alternative to mannitol)
drugs.adultDose: 2.5–5 mL/kg of 3% NaCl IV over 10–15 min.
drugs.preparationIndia: 3% NaCl bags available in most Indian hospitals; can be prepared from 0.9% saline + 15% or 23.4% NaCl per pharmacy protocol.
drugs.cautions: Hypernatraemia, hyperchloraemic acidosis.
